title: Token Lineage & Session Cost Fabric — Exploratory Console Flow
creator: Amelia Chen
description: Discover and prototype a console-first experience that lets engineers and finance owners trace token cost back through session ancestry and model variant decisions. Focus: a lightweight, exportable lineage view (CSV + nested JSON export) that can be dropped into invoices or runbooks. We are intentionally exploring a hybrid UI that mixes timeline, compact calls table, and a visual fabric (graph-lite) that ties tokens -> prompts -> model variant -> route -> rollout. Goal: reduce mean time to explanation for cost spikes and provide a canonical export suitable for reporting and chargeback.
background: Recent support tickets and SLO reviews showed repeated requests for 'why did cost spike for session X' where existing per-route and per-model dashboards were insufficient. Platform telemetry already emits token attribution traces (prefix cache hits, batching deltas, quantization variant), but surface UI is fragmented. This work consolidates those traces into a session-centric lineage canvas that is compact for quick troubleshooting and exportable for accounting teams.
acceptance_criteria: Console shows a session header with summary metrics (tokens, spend, peak latency, model variant history)
Lineage fabric view rendering shows nodes for prompts, completions, cached prefixes, and routing fallbacks
Call table supports filtering/sorting by token cost, latency, model, and timestamp
Export button produces CSV with per-invocation line items and a nested JSON blob containing provenance (model_version, kernel_profile, batch_id)
Prototype validated with at least two PM/Eng teammates and one pilot customer-runbook session
Design handoff assets (Figma + interaction notes) uploaded to Confluence link and linked PR created
design_notes: Primary constraints: keep initial canvas load under 200ms for sessions with <500 invocations. We will lazy-load call details and limit graph breadth by default (show top N branches by cost). Visual language borrows from prior 'timeline + sankey' patterns but prioritizes compactness: small glyphs for cache hits, badges for rollouts, and inline token delta microbars. Consider accessibility: high-contrast color palette and keyboard-first table interactions. Export format needs stable column names for billing ingestion; propose 'invocation_id, session_id, parent_id, model_version, batch_id, tokens_input, tokens_output, cost_usd, timestamp, tags'.
review_comments: PM (Lina Patel): 'Love the session-first approach. Ensure the export has both per-invocation and aggregated session totals for billing ingestion.'
Eng (Kofi Mensah): 'Backend can attach model_version and kernel_profile, but batching metadata is sampled. Will need a flag for full tracing — consider opt-in to avoid storage blowup.'
Eng (Sofia Alvarez): 'We should be explicit about cardinality. Graph rendering must prune low-cost branches by default; add toggle to show all.'
Design (Noah Park): 'Microbars for token deltas are neat; test with colorblind palette. Also add hover states that surface exact token deltas.'
decisions: Prototype will limit graph to top 6 branches by cost by default
Export will contain a two-part payload: flat CSV for accounting and a separate lineage.json with provenance metadata
Tracing flag 'store_full_lineage' will be gated behind Dedicated/Private customer tiers to control storage costs
tradeoffs: Aggressive pruning improves performance but may hide rare low-impact branches that are meaningful for debugging. Full lineage storage provides complete visibility but increases telemetry cost and retention complexity. We favor a tiered approach: default sampling + on-demand full capture for incidents.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: billing teams expect deterministic per-invocation costs but sampling may break that. Mitigation: mark sampled exports clearly and provide sampling-adjusted aggregated totals. Risk: UI complexity — mitigate by progressive disclosure and single-click exports.
